hints: Look closely at the repeat unit in the diagram and work backwards to what small alkene could build that carbon backbone.
Remember that poly(ethene) is just $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$ with no double bonds left, so it cannot be hydrated or oxidised like an alkene.
Think about which polymer would have a good leaving group on every carbon that hydrolysis with aqueous alkali could swap for $\text{-OH}$.
walkthrough:
**Identify the target repeat unit**

Look at the diagram. Every carbon in the chain has one $\text{OH}$ and one $\text{H}$.

So the repeat section is:
$$\text{-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-}$$

**Recall what addition polymerisation leaves behind**

Addition polymerisation opens the $\text{C=C}$ of the monomer to make a saturated $\text{C-C}$ backbone. There are no $\text{C=C}$ bonds left in the polymer.

That means poly(ethene), $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-}_n$, is an unreactive alkane chain. It will not undergo hydration or mild oxidation.

**Test the dichloroethene route**

Polymerise 1,2-dichloroethene, $\text{CHCl=CHCl}$:
$$n\text{CHCl=CHCl} \rightarrow \text{-CHCl-CHCl-}_n$$
Now every carbon carries a $\text{C-Cl}$ bond. Chloroalkanes undergo hydrolysis with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ on heating:
$$\text{-CHCl-CHCl-}_n + 2n\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-}_n + 2n\text{Cl}^-$$
This gives exactly the polyol shown, so this route works.

options.A: Incorrect. Polymerising ethene gives poly(ethene), $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-}_n$. This is a saturated alkane with no $\text{C=C}$ bonds, so hydration (addition of water across a double bond) cannot happen.
options.B: Incorrect. Cold, acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ oxidises $\text{C=C}$ double bonds to diols, but poly(ethene) has no double bonds left after polymerisation. There is nothing to oxidise, so no $\text{-OH}$ groups can be introduced this way.
options.C: Correct. Polymerising $\text{CHCl=CHCl}$ gives $\text{-CHCl-CHCl-}_n$. Each $\text{C-Cl}$ is a chloroalkane group that can be hydrolysed by aqueous alkali to $\text{C-OH}$, giving $\text{-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-}_n$, exactly the structure shown.
options.D: Incorrect. Although polymerising 1,2-dichloroethene gives the right carbon skeleton with Cl substituents, oxidation with cold $\text{KMnO}_4$ requires a $\text{C=C}$ bond. The polymer backbone is saturated, so oxidation does nothing useful. Hydrolysis, not oxidation, is needed to replace Cl with OH.
